solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Foundation: that which splits again

indicators.note: the relative words cut into the word for again, sitting in its middle

parts.note: bis is Latin for twice, used in music to call for a repeat
dialect and old usage has as for that or which, as in 'them as knows'

explanation.surface: A dictionary-style note that a foundation is something that divides once more.
explanation.definitionFit: A basis is the underlying support or groundwork on which something is built.

clue.text: Champion in the past

definitions.meaning: to champion a cause is to support or endorse it
earlier in time, as in years gone by

explanation.surface: A former title holder.
explanation.definitionFit: To back someone is to champion them; something from back then lies in the past.

clue.text: Turner's drink

definitions.meaning: belonging to a turner: the tool with which a person turns screws
a cocktail of vodka and orange juice

explanation.surface: The painter J M W Turner's favourite tipple.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Turner' suggests the painter, but here it is anything that turns, and a screw-turning tool is the possession.
explanation.definitionFit: The tool turns screws, and the cocktail of vodka and orange juice shares its name.

clue.text: Pelt across surface in Innsbruck, heading for gate — doing this?

definitions.text: Pelt across surface in Innsbruck, heading for gate — doing this?

indicators.note: the skin word stretches across the single letter, holding it within

parts.note: a pelt is an animal's skin

indicators.note: the surface of a word is its first letter, its outermost layer
the heading of a word is its opening letter

explanation.surface: Racing down the snow at speed in Innsbruck, aiming for a slalom gate.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue doubles as the definition: someone pelting over the snowy surface of an Austrian resort towards a gate is doing this sport.
explanation.definitionFit: Speeding over snow toward slalom gates in an Alpine resort describes the winter sport on two boards.

clue.text: Guided missile hurt a great deal

parts.note: to smart is to sting or hurt
a bomb is slang for a large sum of money, as in 'cost a bomb'

explanation.surface: A precision weapon that did a lot of damage.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cost a bomb' is British slang for costing a great deal.
explanation.definitionFit: A laser- or satellite-steered explosive dropped on a target is a precision munition.

clue.text: Get large drink — and experience its effect?

parts.note: to see a point is to get it
a double is a twice-sized measure of spirits

explanation.surface: Order a big measure of whisky and suffer the consequences.
explanation.definitionFit: Blurred, twinned vision is a classic symptom of drunkenness, the effect of too much drink.

clue.text: Order has to count in book

indicators.note: put in order means rearranged, so these letters are sorted afresh

explanation.surface: An instruction that one must count something in a ledger.
explanation.walkthrough: 'count' looks like a verb, but it is the noble title: one of Dumas' Three Musketeers.
explanation.definitionFit: The Comte de la Fère, called by his alias, is one of the three musketeers in Dumas' novel.

clue.text: Dense bits of greenery: lettuce caught up in teeth

indicators.note: one piece is placed within the other

parts.note: tusks are long protruding teeth

indicators.note: in a down entry, 'up' means the word is read from the bottom, so the lettuce runs backwards

parts.note: cos is a variety of lettuce, also called romaine

explanation.surface: Salad leaves stuck in someone's teeth.
explanation.definitionFit: Tufts or clumps of coarse grass growing thickly are what the word names.

clue.text: Poem in the dormitory not written down

indicators.note: in a down entry, letters not written downwards run upwards, so they are reversed
the letters sit inside the run of words given

explanation.surface: Verses about the dormitory that nobody wrote out.
explanation.definitionFit: A lyric piece addressed to a subject, like Keats' to a nightingale, is this kind of verse.

clue.text: Top equestrian skill sitting on horse, say?

parts.note: top as an adjective means best
riding is the skill of horsemanship

explanation.surface: Praise for the finest horsemanship.
explanation.definitionFit: To straddle something is to sit astride, legs either side, as a rider does on a mount.

clue.text: Decorative border: ooh, lovely!

parts.note: cor is a British exclamation of surprise
nice means pleasant or lovely

explanation.surface: Someone admiring an ornamental edging.
explanation.walkthrough: COR is a British exclamation like 'gosh'.
explanation.definitionFit: A moulded ledge running round the top of a wall or ceiling is ornamental edging in architecture.

clue.text: Entertainer delivered tango in stockings and smalls

indicators.note: the letter is put within the word for stockings

parts.note: hose is a collective word for stockings
T is tango in the NATO phonetic alphabet
S is the abbreviation for small, so two of them give two letters

explanation.surface: A performer handing over a dance while wearing stockings and underwear.
explanation.walkthrough: 'smalls' is British slang for underwear, but here it is two S abbreviations.
explanation.definitionFit: A woman who receives and looks after guests entertains them.

clue.text: Person not buying story about suspect is down

indicators.note: the tall tale goes round the other letters

parts.note: a whopper is a big lie or story

indicators.note: suspect as an adjective means dubious, so the letters are not in their proper order

explanation.surface: Someone sceptical of a doubtful tale about a suspect being low.
explanation.walkthrough: 'not buying' looks like disbelief, but it literally means browsing without purchasing; 'suspect' scrambles IS DOWN into INDOWS.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone gazing at shop displays without purchasing anything is a browser, literally not buying.

clue.text: Fantastic food that's flying?

definitions.meaning: fanciful, unrealistic, as a hope that will never be realised
a baked dish up in the air, taken literally

explanation.definitionFit: The idiom means an unrealistic hope; literally it would be a pastry dish up among the clouds.

clue.text: Going after leader on bend, dash is admired in perennial silver medallist?:

indicators.note: the scrambled letters follow the single letter
the leader of a word is its first letter
dash as a verb means to smash, so the letters are broken and rearranged

explanation.surface: A racer moving up behind the front-runner at a bend, sprinting, is admired.
explanation.walkthrough: 'dash' scrambles IS ADMIRED; the closing colon is a stray typo. The definition plays on the saying 'always the bridesmaid, never the bride'.
explanation.definitionFit: Always attending but never the bride, like a runner-up who never wins: a perennial second place.

clue.text: Red snapper a restaurateur catches

indicators.note: the words hold the answer within them, as a net catches fish

explanation.surface: A restaurant owner landing a red snapper fish.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Red snapper' reads as a fish, but 'Red' alone is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Meat cooked so lightly it is still pink or bloody inside is described this way.

clue.text: Awful tackling rugby player, that man Charlie

indicators.note: the word for awful takes hold around the other pieces, as a tackler grips a runner

parts.note: awful means bad
a lock is a second-row forward in rugby
he refers to a male person already mentioned

explanation.surface: A dreadful tackle on a rugby player by that fellow Charlie.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Charlie' looks like a name, but in British slang a charlie is a fool.
explanation.definitionFit: Charlie in British slang means a fool or idiot, a dimwit.

clue.text: Away from home regularly, month without roof in flat, perhaps?

parts.note: out means not at home
oft is an old word for often, regularly

indicators.note: in a down entry the roof is the top letter, which is dropped

parts.note: June is a month of the year

explanation.surface: Someone away a lot who has spent a month without a roof over their flat.
explanation.walkthrough: 'flat' looks like an apartment, but it is a musical pitch below the note.
explanation.definitionFit: Singing or playing flat, below the correct pitch, is one way of being off key.

clue.text: Scarlet, I gathered — are those red, did you say?

definitions.note: red sounds like read, so these are items that are read, such as newspaper pieces

indicators.note: gathered together into a new bunch, so the letters are collected in a fresh order

explanation.surface: Musing on a scarlet colour: are those things red?
explanation.walkthrough: 'red' is to be heard as 'read', so the definition is pieces that are read; 'are' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: Newspaper pieces are what readers go through; the definition's sound-alike turns colour into reading.

clue.text: Aquanaut: bloke tending to be different

parts.note: an aquanaut is an underwater explorer, a diver
gent is short for gentleman, a man

explanation.surface: An undersea explorer described as an unconventional fellow.
explanation.definitionFit: Paths that move apart, or views that differ, are described by this adjective.

clue.text: Every second counting, pain found soon

indicators.note: only the second, fourth and later letters count, so alternate letters are taken

explanation.surface: With every second ticking, the pain will be discovered shortly.
explanation.definitionFit: An archaic adverb meaning shortly or presently, as in 'see you later'.

clue.text: Copper on trial, most adorable

parts.note: Cu is the chemical symbol for copper
a test is a trial

explanation.surface: A police officer in the dock who is irresistibly sweet.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Copper' suggests a policeman, but it is the metal's symbol.
explanation.definitionFit: The superlative of a word meaning charming or sweet, so most endearing.

clue.text: Hand upright, empty pan

parts.note: straight means upright, not bent
to flush a lavatory pan is to empty it with water

explanation.surface: Holding up a hand while emptying a cooking pan.
explanation.walkthrough: 'pan' suggests cookware, but here it is a lavatory bowl.
explanation.definitionFit: In poker, five consecutive cards of one suit make the top-ranking holding of cards.

clue.text: Scavenger with bloody tongue on camera, taking every last piece

indicators.note: the final letter of each word is taken

explanation.surface: A wildlife film showing a carrion eater with a bloodied tongue devouring every scrap.
explanation.definitionFit: The African carnivore known for its laugh feeds largely on carcasses left by others.

clue.text: Low sky

definitions.meaning: low means sad or down in spirits
the colour of a clear sky

explanation.definitionFit: Feeling down is feeling this colour; a clear daytime sky shows it.

clue.text: So able, after a tidy up, to keep very clear

indicators.note: the rearranged letters hold the single letter within them
tidied up means rearranged into a new order

explanation.surface: Someone so capable that, after tidying, they keep everything very clean.
explanation.walkthrough: 'after a tidy up' rearranges SO ABLE into ABSOLE, which then keeps V.
explanation.definitionFit: To absolve is to clear someone of blame or guilt, to acquit them.

clue.text: Motto that has teeth

definitions.meaning: a cutting tool with a toothed blade

explanation.definitionFit: An old saying is a maxim or proverb; a carpenter's toothed cutting tool shares the name.

clue.text: Implement unties tangled line

indicators.note: tangled letters are twisted out of their order

explanation.surface: A tool that undoes a knotted rope.
explanation.definitionFit: A kitchen tool, such as a spoon or whisk, is a household implement.

clue.text: Old magistrate coming round wasn't turning towards the camera

indicators.note: the magistrate's title encircles the other letters

parts.note: the doge was the chief magistrate of old Venice and Genoa

indicators.note: turning letters over and round rearranges them

explanation.surface: An elderly judge reviving from a faint, who had not been spinning round towards a lens.
explanation.walkthrough: 'turning' looks like a reversal, but read backwards the letters do not fit; it rearranges them into WNSTA. 'Downstage' is the front of a stage, nearest the audience or camera.
explanation.definitionFit: On a set or stage, moving to the front means toward the audience or lens.

clue.text: Aromatic plant in porridge, reportedly?

indicators.note: as it is reported, spoken, so the word is heard not seen

parts.note: porridge is British slang for time served in prison

explanation.surface: Someone asking whether there is a herb in their porridge oats.
explanation.walkthrough: 'porridge' is British slang for a prison sentence, i.e. time.
explanation.definitionFit: A fragrant culinary herb of the mint family used in cooking.
